title: Light and Shadows
seo_title: Primary 4 Science: Light and Shadows Worksheets (with Answers)
standard_text: Recognise that an object can be seen when it reflects light or when it is a source of light. Recognise that a shadow is formed when light is completely or partially blocked by an object, and investigate how materials let light through (transparent, translucent, opaque) (summary of the MOE Primary Science Syllabus).
meta_desc: Free Primary 4 science worksheets for Singapore pupils on light: light sources, how we see, transparent, translucent and opaque materials, and shadows. 100 questions with answers.
key_big: We see things when light enters our eyes.
key_sub: A shadow forms when an object blocks light.
body_html:
How to think about it

We see an object when light from it enters our eyes. The light is either given out by the object (a light source) or reflected from it.

  • Transparent materials let most light through; translucent materials let some light through; opaque materials let no light through.
  • A shadow forms when an object blocks light. Light travels in straight lines, so the shadow has the outline of the object.
  • The nearer the object is to the light, the bigger its shadow.
Example

Is the Moon a light source?

It does not give out its own light

It reflects light from the Sun

Answer: No.

Example

A toy is moved nearer a torch. What happens to its shadow?

It blocks more of the light

The shadow gets bigger

Answer: It gets bigger.

Common mistakes

  • Thinking the Moon and mirrors are light sources. They only reflect light.
  • Thinking we see because light comes out of our eyes. Light must enter our eyes.
  • Thinking translucent objects make no shadow. They make a lighter shadow.
  • Thinking a shadow gets bigger when the object moves nearer the screen. It gets bigger when the object moves nearer the light.

faq.q: Why is the Moon not a light source?
faq.a: The Moon does not give out its own light. It reflects light from the Sun.

faq.q: What is the difference between translucent and opaque?
faq.a: A translucent material lets some light through, such as frosted glass. An opaque material lets no light through, such as wood or metal.

faq.q: How can I make a shadow bigger?
faq.a: Move the object nearer to the light source, or move the light source nearer to the object.

items.q: What is a translucent material?
c: a material that lets no light through
a material that lets almost all light through
a material that lets some light pass through
a material that gives out light
items.e: Frosted glass and tracing paper are translucent.

items.q: What is a light source?
c: something that gives out its own light
items.e: The Sun, a torch, a candle.

items.q: Is the Moon a light source?
c: not a light source: it reflects light
a light source only at night
items.e: Sources give out light; everything else is seen because it reflects light.

items.q: Which of these is a light source?
items.e: A light source gives out its own light.

items.q: Is a torch that is switched on a light source?
c: not a light source: it reflects light
a light source only at night
items.e: Sources give out light; everything else is seen because it reflects light.

items.q: Which surfaces reflect light best?
items.e: Mirrors and foil.

items.q: What do we need to be able to see things?
items.e: No light, no seeing.

items.q: What is an opaque material?
c: a material that gives out light
a material that does not let light pass through
a material that lets some light through
a material that lets all light through
items.e: Wood and metal are opaque.

items.q: Which shows that light travels in straight lines?
c: Shadows have sharp edges with the same outline as the object.
items.e: Light cannot bend round the object.

items.q: Which of these is NOT a light source: a bicycle reflector, a campfire, a flash of lightning or a star?
items.e: A bicycle reflector does not make its own light; it reflects light.

items.q: How do we see an object that is not a light source, such as a book?
c: We do not need light to see it.
The book gives out its own light.
Light from a light source reflects off the book into our eyes.
Light comes out of our eyes and hits the book.
items.e: Light must enter our eyes.

items.q: What is dark?
items.e: Dark is not a thing; it is no light.

items.q: Why can we see a book, which is not a light source?
c: Our eyes send out light to the book.
Light reflects off the book into our eyes.
items.e: Reflection.

items.q: Is the Moon a light source?
c: Yes, it makes its own light.
No. It reflects light from the Sun.
items.e: Moonlight is reflected sunlight.

items.q: What does reflect mean?
c: bounce light back off a surface
items.e: Like a ball bouncing.

items.q: Is a candle flame a light source?
c: a light source only at night
not a light source: it reflects light
items.e: Sources give out light; everything else is seen because it reflects light.

items.q: Why is the Moon NOT a light source?
c: It reflects light from the Sun.
It is made of rock, so it glows.
items.e: The Moon has no light of its own.

items.q: Is a mirror a light source?
c: No. It reflects light very well.
items.e: Shiny is not the same as glowing.

items.q: Which of these is NOT a light source: a candle flame, a lit bulb, a sheet of white paper or the Sun?
items.e: A sheet of white paper does not make its own light; it reflects light.

items.q: Which of these is NOT a light source: a campfire, a torch that is switched on, the Sun or the planet Venus?
c: a torch that is switched on
items.e: The planet Venus does not make its own light; it reflects light.

items.q: Which would help you be seen walking on a dark road?
items.e: Reflect the light.

items.q: Which of these reflects the least light: a navy blue towel, a polished silver tray, a sheet of kitchen foil or a still pond?
items.e: Dark, dull and rough surfaces reflect very little light.

items.q: In a room with no light at all, could you see a toy car?
c: No. With no light, no light can reflect from it into your eyes.
Yes, if you wait for your eyes to get used to it.
Yes, if it is shiny or white.
Yes, a little, because objects glow.
items.e: We see objects when light reflects off them into our eyes. Dark is the absence of light.

items.q: Why do cyclists wear reflective strips at night?
c: The strips make their own light.
Car headlights reflect off them, so drivers can see the cyclist.
items.e: Be seen, be safe.

items.q: Which of these is NOT a light source: a campfire, a candle flame, a cat's eye reflector on a road or the Sun?
c: a cat's eye reflector on a road
items.e: A cat's eye reflector on a road does not make its own light; it reflects light.

items.q: Which of these reflects the least light: a dark carpet, a new coin, a sheet of kitchen foil or a still pond?
items.e: Dark, dull and rough surfaces reflect very little light.

items.q: Why can you see yourself in a still pond but not in a choppy one?
c: Choppy water is a light source.
A smooth surface reflects light evenly; a rough one scatters it.
items.e: Smooth reflects clearly.

items.q: Why are school high-visibility jackets bright yellow or orange?
c: Bright colours are easy to see, and the strips reflect light.
items.e: Safety.

items.q: In a room with no light at all, could you see a clock on the wall?
c: Yes, if it is shiny or white.
Yes, if you wait for your eyes to get used to it.
No. With no light, no light can reflect from it into your eyes.
Yes, a little, because objects glow.
items.e: We see objects when light reflects off them into our eyes. Dark is the absence of light.

items.q: In a room with no light at all, could you see a book?
c: No. With no light, no light can reflect from it into your eyes.
Yes, if you wait for your eyes to get used to it.
Yes, a little, because objects glow.
Yes, if it is shiny or white.
items.e: We see objects when light reflects off them into our eyes. Dark is the absence of light.

items.q: Why does kitchen foil look brighter when it is flat than when it is scrunched up?
c: A flat, smooth surface reflects light back more evenly.
Flat foil is a light source.
items.e: Smooth surfaces.

items.q: Which would be best to make a sign that is easy to see at night?
items.e: Reflects headlights.

items.q: Which of these reflects the least light: a bicycle reflector, a black woollen sweater, a mirror or a polished silver tray?
items.e: Dark, dull and rough surfaces reflect very little light.

items.q: What are 'cat's eyes' on roads?
c: small reflectors that show drivers where the lanes are
items.e: Invented in Britain.

items.q: Why do road signs reflect car headlights at night?
c: to light up the whole road
so drivers can read them in the dark
items.e: Reflective paint.

items.q: Which of these reflects the least light: a bicycle reflector, a glossy white tile, a lump of black coal or a new coin?
items.e: Dark, dull and rough surfaces reflect very little light.

items.q: You hold a book up to a mirror. What happens to the writing?
c: It appears back to front (reversed left to right).
items.e: Mirror images are reversed.

items.q: Which of these is NOT a light source: a cat's eye reflector on a road, a glowing computer screen, a star or a torch that is switched on?
c: a cat's eye reflector on a road
a torch that is switched on
items.e: A cat's eye reflector on a road does not make its own light; it reflects light.

items.q: How many mirrors does a simple periscope use?
items.e: One at the top and one at the bottom.

items.q: Which of these is NOT a light source: a firefly, a lit bulb, a shiny spoon or a star?
items.e: A shiny spoon does not make its own light; it reflects light.

items.q: How does light travel?
items.e: Rays of light are straight.

items.q: Is cardboard transparent, translucent or opaque?
items.e: Cardboard lets no light through and makes a dark shadow.

items.q: Is a metal tray transparent, translucent or opaque?
items.e: A metal tray lets no light through and makes a dark shadow.

items.q: Why should you never look directly at the Sun?
c: It is not a light source.
It is too far away to see.
Its light is so strong it can damage your eyes.
items.e: Safety.

items.q: Which material would make the darkest shadow?
items.e: Opaque materials block all the light.

items.q: Which material would make the darkest shadow?
items.e: Opaque materials block all the light.

items.q: Why does the Moon look bright at night?
c: It reflects light from the Sun.
items.e: The Moon is not a light source.

items.q: Three cards with holes are lined up so you can see a torch through them. One card is moved. What happens?
c: The light bends to reach you.
You can no longer see the torch.
items.e: Light travels in straight lines.

items.q: Which travels faster: light or sound?
c: they travel at the same speed
items.e: Light is about a million times faster.

items.q: Why do we see lightning before we hear thunder?
c: Light travels much faster than sound.
items.e: They happen at the same time.

items.q: A material lets almost all light through, so you can see clearly through it. Which word describes it?
items.e: Transparent, translucent, opaque.

items.q: Is frosted glass transparent, translucent or opaque?
items.e: Frosted glass lets some light through, but you cannot see clearly through it.

items.q: Is cling film transparent, translucent or opaque?
items.e: Cling film lets almost all light through, so you can see clearly through it.

items.q: What is darkness?
items.e: No light reaching our eyes.

items.q: Which material would make the darkest shadow?
items.e: Opaque materials block all the light.

items.q: A material lets some light through, but you cannot see clearly through it. Which word describes it?

items.q: Is tissue paper transparent, translucent or opaque?

items.q: Is aluminium foil transparent, translucent or opaque?
items.e: Aluminium foil lets no light through and makes a dark shadow.

items.q: Is a shadow a reflection?
c: Yes, it is a dark mirror image.
No. A shadow is where light is blocked, not bounced back.
items.e: Different things.

c: a dark area where light is blocked by an object
items.e: Light cannot get through.
